disclaimer: Reminder reference only - NOT legal authority. Season dates, zones, and limits are set annually and can change. Always verify current regulations with the Saskatchewan Ministry of Environment before hunting or trapping. Trapping in Saskatchewan is governed by The Wildlife Act, 1998, The Wildlife Regulations, 1981 (W-13.1 Reg 1) and The Fur Animals Open Seasons Regulations (W-13.12 Reg 4). This dataset is for the separate Canada clone of Opossum Foot; it is NOT part of the US app, which stays US-only and untouched.

license_summary.certified_traps: Saskatchewan adopts the Fur Institute of Canada certified-trap lists by reference: 'certified trap' and 'certified restraining trap' are defined as traps on the FIC lists certified under AIHTS (The Wildlife Regulations, 1981, s. 2(h.11) and (h.12)). See the 'aihts' section of this dataset.
license_summary.course: First-time trappers must satisfy s. 33(1)(a): be a Saskatchewan resident, hold a firearm safety/hunter education certificate, and either obtain a mark set by the minister on a minister-approved trapping examination, have previously held a lawful trapping licence in Saskatchewan or elsewhere, or have completed a minister-approved trapping course. In practice: a recognized humane trapper education course or an equivalency test at a Ministry of Environment office (pass mark 75%). Courses are delivered by the Saskatchewan Trappers Association in the south and the Northern Saskatchewan Trappers Association in the north. Persons born after January 1, 1971 must graduate from a firearm safety/hunter education course to hold a fur licence. Youth aged 12 to 15 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian when using a firearm while trapping; youth under 16 may not use a firearm while trapping.
license_summary.fees: Southern Fur Conservation Area Fur Licence $45; Northern Fur Conservation Area Fur Licence $25; Saskatchewan Resident Youth Fur Licence no fee; Saskatchewan Treaty Indian Fur Licence no fee (The Wildlife Regulations, 1981, Table 3, includes GST; confirmed on saskatchewan.ca). Saskatchewan Wildlife Habitat Licence $20 including GST (s. 37.1); Veteran Wildlife Habitat Licence $0 (s. 37.11). Resident Fur Dealer Licence $65 plus an agent fee (maximum 3 agents); Non-resident Fur Dealer Licence $480 (Table 3).
license_summary.fur_conservation_areas: The province is split into two fur conservation areas (The Wildlife Regulations, 1981, s. 55): the Northern Fur Conservation Area (NFCA) - non-leased provincial land north of the Highway 3 / Highway 35 / Highway 49 line to the Manitoba border, plus the North Saskatchewan River / Township 44 block and Duck Mountain Provincial Park - and the Southern Fur Conservation Area (SFCA), the rest of the province. The NFCA is divided into trapping blocks (88 in 1946, per the ministry Fur Program summary), each run by its members through a Representative Council of up to 5 members (s. 56) with a certificate of registration and map (s. 57). A trapper must be voted in by block members to trap there; a licence holder inactive for two years relinquishes block privileges (s. 58). Unallocated vacant Crown land north of the block line is treated as NFCA special areas, open without block membership (ministry Fur Program summary).
license_summary.harvest_report: There is no Ontario-style season-end harvest report filed by individual trappers. Harvest is monitored through Fur Dealer Returns of Pelts Purchased (dealers report monthly, by the 5th, under s. 41) and Fur Export Permits. The minister may require a licence holder to complete and return a hunter harvest survey as a licence condition (s. 31.4); the Annual Status of Furbearers Survey runs March 1 to April 30 each year. NFCA trappers must provide the director, on request, any information the director requires (s. 59(2)).
license_summary.hunting_furbearers: A fur licence holder may hunt fur animals other than bears or cougars with a firearm during an open fur season, provided they are not accompanying or assisting a big game hunter. Cougar may be harvested under a fur licence by trap or snare only; a firearm may only dispatch a cougar already restrained (s. 25(2)(b)). Black bear under a fur licence: in the NFCA only by a trapper conducting normal bear-trapping operations; in the SFCA only after the bear is restrained in a mechanically activated foot snare (s. 25(2)(a)). Saskatchewan residents may hunt coyotes with a firearm without a licence (s. 32(3) in the SFCA; s. 36(5)). Raccoons and skunks may be hunted without a licence outside special areas (s. 4(1)(f), (g)).
license_summary.licence_types: Southern Fur Conservation Area Fur Licence; Northern Fur Conservation Area Fur Licence (valid only in the trapping block or zone specified on the licence, s. 34); Saskatchewan Resident Youth Fur Licence (free; ages 12 to 19, s. 37.2; same rights as an SFCA or NFCA licence); Saskatchewan Treaty Indian Fur Licence (free; valid only for sale of furs taken on an Indian Reserve). SFCA licences may be bought through HAL (www.saskatchewanhal.ca) or at Ministry offices; NFCA and youth licences only at Ministry of Environment field offices.
license_summary.licence_validity: Fur licences go on sale April 1 through HAL and at Ministry offices. A fur licence plus a Wildlife Habitat Licence is valid for trapping and possessing unprocessed fur until August 31 following the date of issue (s. 31(11)).
license_summary.pelt_sale_export: A fur licence (or fur dealer licence, special permit, or Treaty Indian Fur Licence) is required to sell unprocessed pelts or parts of fur animals (s. 32(1.1)). A Fur Export Permit is required before shipping or moving raw fur pelts out of Saskatchewan to another province or country (The Wildlife Act, 1998, s. 31(1)). A CITES permit is additionally required to ship pelts or parts of black bear, bobcat, lynx, otter and wolf across international borders. Shipments of wildlife must be tagged or marked with the owner's name and address, the licence number under which the wildlife was taken, and the contents (s. 53).
license_summary.permission: Southern fur conservation area: trap only on land where you have permission from the landowner or occupant (or the controlling government agency for Crown land); consent rules under The Wildlife Act, 1998, s. 41 and The Wildlife Regulations, 1981, s. 6.01. Northern fur conservation area: trap only in the trapping block or zone on your licence, and only as a voted-in block member (ss. 34, 55-57). Landowners and occupants have prior trapping rights on waters bordering their land in the SFCA (s. 35). No traps or firearms within 500 metres of an occupied building, stockade or corral without the owner's consent (s. 13). Fur licences are not valid in national parks; trapping in most provincial parks requires the written authority of the park manager.
license_summary.quotas: No bag or possession limits are set in The Fur Animals Open Seasons Regulations. Harvest is controlled in the northern fur conservation area by licence-stated limits: the director may limit the number of fur animals a licensee may take in a trapping block or zone, and no holder shall take more than the number stated on his or her fur licence without the director's prior authorization (s. 59).
license_summary.report_violation: Turn in Poachers and Polluters (TIPP) line 1-800-667-7561, 24 hours, 7 days a week (saskatchewan.ca).
license_summary.snares: Nets and snares for fur animals require a licence for the purpose, except snares for rabbits or squirrels, snares under ice, and mechanically activated foot snares (s. 24(1)). Free-hanging neck snares require a Special Permit from the ministry; they may not be used in the southern fur conservation area except for livestock predation control. Power snares and power-assisted snares require a licence issued by the director under s. 6(2) (s. 24(2)(j)). All snares must have a locking device (s. 24(2)(h)).
license_summary.trap_check: Return to every trap or snare to check it: at least every 24 hours if set in the southern fur conservation area in a town or city with a population over 1,000 people or within 5 km of one, and for mechanically activated foot snares set for black bear in the southern fur conservation area; at least every 72 hours elsewhere in the southern fur conservation area; at least every 120 hours in the northern fur conservation area (s. 24(3)).
license_summary.trapping_licence: A fur licence is required to hunt any fur animal (The Wildlife Regulations, 1981, s. 32(1)), together with a Saskatchewan Wildlife Habitat Licence or a Veteran Wildlife Habitat Licence. Fur licences are available to Saskatchewan residents only (s. 31(2)(a); s. 33(1)(a)). A fur licence plus a habitat licence is valid for trapping and possessing unprocessed fur until August 31 following the date of issue (s. 31(11)).

aihts.note: Saskatchewan implements AIHTS by incorporating the Fur Institute of Canada certified-trap lists by reference in the definitions: a 'certified trap' is a body-gripping trap on the FIC list of quick-kill traps certified under the Agreement on International Humane Trapping Standards, and a 'certified restraining trap' is a foot-hold trap on the FIC list of restraining traps certified under the Agreement, in each case as published and updated from time to time by the Fur Institute of Canada (The Wildlife Regulations, 1981, s. 2(h.11) and (h.12)). Section 24(2)(k) makes certified body-gripping traps mandatory for beaver, bobcat, otter, lynx, marten, fisher, ermine, least weasel, long-tailed weasel, muskrat and raccoon. Section 24(2)(i) separately requires a certified restraining trap for any foot-hold trap set on land for live capture and restraint of any fur animal (or, where no trap is certified for the species, a trap modified to improve humaneness). AIHTS was agreed in 1997 and ratified by Canada in June 1999; it covers 12 North American species. Phase 1 regulated species in Saskatchewan are coyote, wolf, lynx, bobcat, beaver, otter, muskrat, marten, fisher, raccoon, badger and short-tailed weasel (ermine). Phase 2 species are not yet regulated.
trap_rules: Body-gripping traps must be certified traps for beaver, bobcat, otter, lynx, marten, fisher, ermine, least weasel, long-tailed weasel, muskrat and raccoon (s. 24(2)(k)).
A foot-hold trap used on land for live capture and restraint must be a certified restraining trap, or, where no trap is certified for the species, a trap modified to improve humaneness (s. 24(2)(i)).
Traps with an inside jaw spread exceeding 24 cm are prohibited (s. 24(2)(d)); no serrated teeth or jaws (s. 24(2)(e)); no hooks or sharp devices to snag or spear fur animals (s. 24(2)(f)).
Foot-hold traps set in water for beaver, otter, mink or muskrat must be set so the animal drowns when caught (s. 24(2)(c)).
Every snare must be equipped with a locking device to prevent the noose from opening (s. 24(2)(h)).
No trap or snare may be left set for a fur animal after the close of that animal's open season (s. 24(2)(b)).

Trap check: at least every 24 hours if set in the southern fur conservation area in a town or city with a population over 1,000 people or within 5 km of one, and for mechanically activated foot snares set for black bear in the southern fur conservation area; at least every 72 hours elsewhere in the southern fur conservation area; at least every 120 hours in the northern fur conservation area (s. 24(3)).
Black bear may only be taken with mechanically activated foot snares (s. 24(1.1)).

Free-hanging neck snares require a Special Permit from the ministry; they may not be used in the southern fur conservation area except for livestock predation control; permit snares must come from a ministry-approved supplier and be tagged with the trapper's HAL number or name and phone number (ministry Fur Program summary).
Power snares and power-assisted snares require a licence issued by the director under s. 6(2) (s. 24(2)(j)).
Spring-pole sets on poles or trees must be set to kill the animal with reasonable dispatch (s. 24(2)(g)).
No person shall touch or interfere with any legally placed trap or snare unless authorized by the owner (s. 24(2)(a)).

aihts.canada_wide: AIHTS in force in Canada since 1 June 1999 (Canada, the EU and Russia are parties; the US is not a party). FIC-certified traps mandatory per Phase 1 lists - killing traps: beaver, Canada lynx & bobcat, fisher, marten, muskrat (on land and underwater), otter, raccoon, weasels/ermine; restraining traps: beaver (cage), bobcat, Canada lynx, raccoon, wolf. Conventional steel-jawed leghold restraining traps on land are effectively banned for AIHTS species. Killing neck snares are NOT AIHTS traps and are not FIC-certified; provinces regulate snares separately. [R1 s.2a]

check_interval.live_holding: 24 hours within 5 km of a town/city over 1,000 people (outside the Fur Conservation Block) and for black bear sets; 72 hours in the Southern Fur Conservation Area beyond that; 120 hours (5 days) in the Northern Fur Conservation Area (Wildlife Regulations s. 24(3)).
check_interval.killing: Same intervals - Saskatchewan does not split check intervals by trap type in s. 24(3).

canada_only.tenure: Two macro-zones: the Northern Fur Conservation Area (fur-block membership - a fur licence can only be bought by members of an existing northern fur block) vs the Southern Fur Conservation Area (open to licensed residents, private-land/permission based). Fur licences are Saskatchewan-resident-only.
canada_only.trap_id_requirement: None found - no trap owner-ID marking requirement in the sources searched (follow-up pass, Nov 17); identification runs through licence/tenure and pelt seals instead. A HAL identification number may identify hunting baits and stands on Crown land - not traps.
canada_only.royalty: No royalty currently charged - the per-pelt royalty was removed for 2011/12 (ministerial answer tabled in the Legislative Assembly, March 28, 2011). [R2 Item 5]
canada_only.nuisance_route: Paid route exists, producer/RM-driven - under the SARM/RM Beaver Control Program, trapping a nuisance beaver requires the RM or First Nation band to contract a trapper holding a valid trapping licence; SCIC hires predation specialists where livestock predation persists. Coyotes may be shot year-round in the SFCA without a licence, but trapping them requires a fur licence plus landowner permission. [R1 s.4]
